summary: Recommends a practice for revoking posting rights to IETF mailing lists for people who engage in bad faith disruption. It gives the IETF a way to manage participant interaction when a person attacks its consensus process. It is a best current practice that has been replaced by RFC 9945.

plainLanguage.summary: If one person keeps interrupting the IETF's discussions on purpose so that no group can finish, the IESG needs a fair way to ask that person to stop posting. This RFC describes that way: a formal vote on the IETF's usual terms, with a minimum length of one year and a right of appeal.

subtitle: How the IETF can remove a disruptive person's right to post to its mailing lists.

tldr.problem: A small number of participants have disrupted the IETF's consensus-driven process by repeatedly posting off-topic or inflammatory messages to its mailing lists.
tldr.mechanism: The IESG may approve a new kind of action, a PR-action, that removes named people's posting rights, using its normal last call and consensus steps.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3683 has been replaced by RFC 9945, and it was also updated by RFC 9245.

today: RFC 3683 is a Best Current Practice that has been obsoleted by RFC 9945 and updated by RFC 9245.

sections.title: Why a Revocation Practice Was Needed
sections.content:
The IETF develops computer-communications standards in an open fashion through a consensus-driven process, and mailing lists are used pervasively for that discussion. Unlike many other organizations, anyone may post messages on IETF mailing lists, and in doing so participates in the process. Historically this has worked very well, because it fosters participation from a wide range of stakeholders.

In a small number of cases, a participant has engaged in what amounts to a denial-of-service attack on the consensus-driven process, typically by repeatedly posting messages that are off-topic, inflammatory or otherwise counter-productive. This is different from good faith disagreement, which is a healthy part of the process. If a working group is unable to reach consensus, that is an acceptable outcome; if it fails to achieve consensus because it is being continuously disrupted, then the disruption constitutes an abuse of the process.

Guidelines for dealing with abusive behaviour already exist, and in practice their application has included the temporary suspension of posting rights to a specific mailing list, with the length of the suspension increased on each successive suspension. When those guidelines fail to change the behaviour, more drastic measures should be available to reduce or eliminate the impact of such attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Disagreeing with a group's decision is normal and healthy. Someone who keeps posting off-topic or inflammatory messages so that the group can never finish is a different problem, and the IETF needed a fair way to deal with it.

sections.title: The PR-action
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) makes decisions called actions, typically the publication of a document on the standards track, the chartering of a working group, and so on. This memo recommends that the IESG also undertake a new type of action, termed a PR-action, which means a posting rights action.

A PR-action identifies one or more individuals, citing messages posted by those individuals to an IETF mailing list that appear to be abusive of the consensus-driven process. If approved by the IESG, then the people named on the action have their posting rights to that IETF mailing list removed, and maintainers of any IETF mailing list may, at their discretion, also remove posting rights to that list.

Once taken, this action remains in force until explicitly nullified and SHOULD remain in force for at least one year. One year after a PR-action is approved, a new PR-action MAY be introduced which restores the posting rights for that individual, and the IESG SHOULD consider the frequency of nullifying requests when evaluating a new PR-action. If the posting rights are restored, the individual is responsible for contacting the owners of the mailing lists to have them restored.
sections.plainLanguage: The IESG can vote to remove someone's right to post to a list. The removal lasts at least a year, and only a further vote from the IESG can lift it.

sections.title: How a PR-action Is Decided
sections.content:
Whether the action revokes or restores posting rights, the IESG follows the same algorithm it uses for its other actions.

  1. It is introduced by an IESG Area Director, who, prior to doing so, may choose to inform the interested parties.
  2. It is published as an IESG last call on the IETF general discussion list.
  3. It is discussed by the community.
  4. It is discussed by the IESG.
  5. Using the usual consensus-based process, it is decided upon by the IESG.

As with all IESG actions, the appeals process outlined in RFC 2026 may be invoked to contest a PR-action approved by the IESG. Working groups SHOULD ensure that their associated mailing list is manageable, and because some people may try to circumvent a revocation by changing email addresses, it should be possible to restrict the new address.
sections.plainLanguage: The decision goes through the same steps as any other IETF decision: someone proposes it, the whole list discusses it, the IESG discusses it, and the IESG decides. The person can still appeal the outcome.

sections.title: Security Considerations and the Limits of a PR-action
sections.content:
A PR-action deals solely with posting rights. Consistent with the final paragraph of Section 3.2 of the IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures, no action may be taken to prevent individuals from receiving messages sent to a mailing list.

The Security Considerations section says that the memo deals with matters of process, not protocol, and notes that it describes a mechanism to throttle active denial-of-service attacks against the consensus-driven process used by the IETF.

The appendix is a short set of questions and answers. It argues that a year is not too long, because an initial PR-action is approved only after a period of substantive consideration and community review. It says a single action should cover all IETF lists, since requiring one per list would enable a prolonged series of attacks. It says the initiation of a PR-action comes informally from outside the IESG but formally always from an IESG Area Director. And it says the rules around PR-actions exhibit the same properties as the rest of the consensus-based process.
sections.plainLanguage: The person can still read the list, they just cannot send to it. These are rules about how people behave, not about how the mail server is configured.

items.title: Isn't a year too long?
items.text: No. A PR-action is approved only after substantive consideration and community review, which indicates that a serious situation has arisen.

items.title: Why not one action per list?
items.text: Because that would enable a prolonged series of denial-of-service attacks. Someone who behaves poorly on one IETF list is unlikely to behave well on another.

items.title: Should the action come from outside the IESG?
items.text: Informally, yes; formally, no. IESG actions are always formally initiated by an IESG Area Director, though the motivation usually comes from outside.

items.title: What is a PR-action about?
items.text: Posting rights only. No action may stop an individual from receiving the messages sent to a mailing list.
